synopsis: StageWAM supplies a Motus world–action model with an instruction-conditioned latent target for the next inferred manipulation stage. A separately trained V-JEPA2 predictor produces this target; a gated residual then conditions video tokens, influencing both video and action generation through joint attention. The authors report 90.25% overall RoboTwin success. Reader assessment: the ablations support adding the conditioning pathway more strongly than they establish the benefit of stage-specific prediction, whose supervision also contains substantial temporal overlap. [e04, e05, e06, e10, e11, e13]

problem.text: The authors argue that fixed video–action chunks describe local scene evolution while leaving the next task-relevant object state or relation implicit. They seek a latent progress target that can guide local control without requiring pixel reconstruction or an explicit transition duration.

contributions.text: A formulation separates short-term physical prediction from a semantic target for the next task stage.
Stage-JEPA learns current-to-next-boundary representations from automatically constructed demonstration pairs, without manual stage annotations.
A bounded, global gate introduces the predicted stage representation into a Motus video stream; the full system is evaluated in simulation and in two physical manipulation tasks.

inputs: Visual observations, robot state and linguistic task instruction for the WAM. [e02, e05]
Centered 64-frame demonstration slices during Stage-I training; a causal 64-frame observation buffer during deployment. [e03, e08]
outputs: A predicted next-stage latent, pooled from 256 target tokens. [e04]
Eight future video frames and 16 predicted actions; execution uses a finite action chunk followed by renewed observation. [e07, e08]

steps.name: Infer demonstration boundaries
steps.detail: Sample candidate centers every eight frames, include the terminal frame, and uniformly reduce the list to at most 32 centers. Frozen V-JEPA2 encodes centered 64-frame clips. Compare candidates two list positions apart on either side using pooled-feature distance and maximum corresponding-token distance. Smooth and independently normalize both scores, take their maximum, then apply non-maximum suppression with radius three candidate positions to retain at most five transition centers.

steps.name: Construct dense stage targets
steps.detail: Add episode endpoints to the selected boundaries. Pair every frame within an interval with its next boundary. Both current and target clips use offsets −32 through 31, with endpoint clipping. These are contextual clips surrounding feature-derived boundaries, rather than manually verified semantic states.

steps.name: Learn the latent predictor
steps.detail: Freeze the V-JEPA2 encoder and train its pretrained predictor plus an instruction cross-attention adapter. From 8,192 encoder tokens of dimension 1,024, uniformly sample 512 context positions and 256 target positions. Mean-pool and normalize predicted and target representations for cosine alignment.

steps.name: Condition joint world–action generation
steps.detail: Freeze Stage-JEPA. Motus combines a Wan2.2-initialized video expert, an action expert and an understanding stream using a frozen Qwen3-VL encoder. Layerwise joint attention exchanges information between streams. Separately noised video latents and demonstrated actions are processed to predict their flow fields.

steps.name: Inject stage guidance
steps.detail: Mean-pool predicted stage tokens, project them through an MLP, and add the resulting vector to video tokens before transformer processing. The vector varies by sample; its bounded scalar gate is shared across samples, tokens, channels and layers. Action generation receives stage information through the interacting WAM streams.

training.text: Stage I uses AdamW for 1,000 updates with learning rate 1e-5, weight decay 0.01 and 100 warmup updates. Frozen encoding uses FP16; trainable modules use FP32. Eight A800 80GB GPUs provide effective batch size 256.

Stage II trains the WAM and conditioning interface for four epochs in BF16, with learning rate 1e-6, weight decay 0.01, 200 warmup updates and effective batch size 256. Video and action losses have unit weights. Gate regularization uses lambda_g=1e-4, lambda_rho=1e-3 and target relative injection magnitude rho_0=0.08; the gate starts at 0.02.
Action targets occur at raw-frame offsets 3, 6, …, 48; video targets at 6, 12, …, 48, with video resolution 384×320. Both stages are trained once with seed 0, and their final checkpoints are used.

inference.text: Maintain observed history only, repeating the earliest frame until the 64-frame buffer is full. Predict a stage latent, condition joint video/action generation, execute a finite action chunk, append observations and repeat. Demonstration boundaries and target clips are unavailable at deployment.
The learned action output drives execution. The described procedure does not select actions by searching generated videos or applying inverse dynamics to a predicted goal image.

equations.expression: Yhat_t^stage = f_theta(o_t, l); p_phi(V_t^short, A_t | o_t, s_t, l, Yhat_t^stage)
equations.explanation: Equations (3)–(4) add a predicted stage condition to the joint distribution over future video V and action chunk A. Observation, state and instruction are o, s and l. Deployment instantiates the predictor with causal history H_t in Eq. (15).
Equation (9) minimizes cosine discrepancy between normalized predicted and target representations over batch size B. Supervision aligns latent representations without reconstructing target pixels.

equations.expression: h_t = P_psi(Pool(Zhat_t^target)); alpha = 0.2 sigmoid(beta); Xtilde_t^v = X_t^v + alpha h_t
equations.explanation: Equations (10)–(12) project the pooled stage prediction into video-token dimension. The sample-specific vector h_t is broadcast across video tokens, while a single learned scalar beta bounds the gate alpha between zero and 0.2.

results.setting: Clean and randomized configurations; 100 closed-loop episodes per task–configuration pair, totaling 10,000 episodes per checkpoint
results.comparison: Published Motus results: 88.66 clean and 87.02 randomized; calculated gains are 2.76 and 2.06 percentage points.
results.interpretation: These measure executed simulated-task success. Baseline values are imported from Motus; the authors state that StageWAM and Motus use the same closed-loop protocol.

results.setting: Two RoboTwin tasks; unweighted task means under clean and randomized evaluation
results.interpretation: This is a particularly strong category-level gain. Reader analysis: the two-task grouping provides limited evidence for the broader claim that stage guidance specifically benefits relational transitions.

results.setting: RoboTwin; overall success averaged across 50 tasks and both configurations
results.value: Reported: full model 90.25; without JEPA 87.23; current-frame-token guidance only 89.89; without Stage-I training 89.98; without gate regularizers 89.88
results.comparison: Calculated: removing the whole JEPA pathway costs 3.02 percentage points; Stage-I optimization adds 0.27 percentage points over its ablation.
results.interpretation: Reader analysis: the extra pathway contributes substantially more than task-specific predictor training. No reported uncertainty establishes whether the smaller differences are stable. The no-JEPA ablation is distinct from the published Motus baseline.

results.setting: Closed-loop evaluation; successful episodes terminate on success, while failures continue to the evaluation horizon
results.value: Reported StageWAM: 132.80 across all rollouts and 74.82 among successful rollouts
results.comparison: Motus: 156.28 and 79.57 respectively; reported reductions are 15.02% and 5.97%.
results.interpretation: All-rollout averages combine execution length with success frequency. Reader analysis: successful-only averages still condition on different sets of successes and do not establish matched-episode or wall-clock speed improvements.

results.setting: LIFT2 dual-arm platform; 20 trials per task; separate task models trained using 50 and 116 trajectories respectively
results.metric: Mean terminal task-progress score on a 0–100 scale
results.value: Reported StageWAM: Cube_Grasp 45.00, Power_Strip 51.00, unweighted average 48.00
results.interpretation: These are physical-execution results using task-specific ordinal progress scores, with safety failures scored zero. They are not completion percentages; the supplied averages cannot recover full-task success rates.

limitations.text: Centered training clips can include future observations relative to their center, whereas deployment is causal. Current and target clips overlap in 86.77% of clean pairs and 86.34% of randomized pairs. Reader concern: shared content may simplify latent prediction and create a training–inference mismatch; deployment itself is documented as using observed history only.

Feature-change boundaries are not validated semantic annotations. Mean inferred stage length is 44.74 raw frames, while WAM targets already extend to frame offset 48. The experiments therefore establish a different conditioning representation more clearly than a systematically longer prediction horizon.

Single-seed training and absent uncertainty limit interpretation of small ablation gains. The physical study covers only two separately trained tasks and lacks a Motus comparison, leaving broad physical generalization and the WAM-specific benefit unresolved.

Benefits are not uniform: acquisition/lifting trails Motus in both settings. The authors identify precise contact, constrained motion and timing as remaining challenges, and propose reducing inference latency and improving fine-grained latent representations.
Tables 1 and 6 print inconsistent clean aggregate values for GO-1 and X-VLA. Those aggregates are excluded from this report's comparisons; the Motus and StageWAM aggregates agree.

reproduction.text: Reconstruct stage pairs with candidate-list subsampling, smoothing, endpoint clipping and NMS measured in candidate positions. Match the supplied token sampling, raw-frame target offsets, frozen modules, training schedules and final-checkpoint selection; these details materially define the experiment.

The supplied text leaves exact WAM checkpoint selection, denoising solver settings, instruction-adapter/MLP implementation, train–evaluation instance separation and physical control timing insufficiently specified for an exact reproduction. Code was not inspected and experiments were not reproduced.

A focused mechanism test would compare matched conditioning models using pretrained features, centered next-boundary supervision and causal-history next-boundary supervision. Repeat seeds and measure success, latent prediction error and latency to separate representation benefits from overlapping-window supervision.

reasoning.text: The recorded Q3 classification is supported: a separately trained, frozen Stage-JEPA predictor feeds a distinct Motus generator, and that generator jointly predicts video and actions. Stage guidance remains active during inference rather than serving only as an auxiliary loss. Latent prediction/JEPA and joint video–action modeling are directly supported. The memory/long-horizon tag needs qualification: the demonstrated memory mechanism is a causal observation buffer, and inferred stages are often short; no separate learned long-term memory mechanism is described.

discussionQuestions: Does the Stage-I gain persist when current training clips contain only causal history and current–target overlap is controlled? [e11, e13]
Do inferred boundaries outperform fixed-offset targets under matched data, architecture and training budgets? [e03, e07]
Would direct stage conditioning of action tokens improve contact-sensitive tasks compared with guidance mediated through video tokens? [e05, e06, e17]
Do shorter successful rollouts yield lower physical completion time once Stage-JEPA and WAM inference latency are included? [e12, e17]

evidence.location: PDF p. 1, title, author list and arXiv version line
evidence.detail: The supplied title, identifier and all nine authors match the catalog. The title page identifies the artifact as arXiv:2608.10780v3, dated 14 Aug 2026.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 1–2, Introduction; p. 3, Task Formulation, Eqs. (1)–(4)
evidence.detail: The authors distinguish local video–action futures from next-stage semantic targets and formulate joint video/action prediction conditioned on a predicted stage latent.

evidence.location: PDF p. 3, Stage-pair construction, Eqs. (5)–(8); p. 10, Implementation Details—Stage-pair construction
evidence.detail: These passages specify candidate spacing and subsampling, centered clips, smoothed feature-change scores, candidate-position NMS, dense next-boundary pairs and endpoint repetition. The boundaries are automatic rather than manual stage labels.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 3–4, Goal-conditioned stage prediction and Eq. (9); p. 10, Gate and token sampling
evidence.detail: Frozen V-JEPA2 encodes current and target clips. A trainable predictor and instruction adapter learn normalized latent alignment. The appendix specifies 8,192 encoder tokens, dimension 1,024, 512 context positions and 256 predicted target positions.

evidence.location: PDF p. 4, Stage II: Training the Stage-Conditioned WAM
evidence.detail: Stage-JEPA is frozen. Motus uses video, action and understanding experts with joint attention, a Wan2.2-initialized video expert and frozen Qwen3-VL encoding. Video and action heads predict flow fields from separately noised targets.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 4–5, conditioning interface, Eqs. (10)–(14) and explanatory paragraphs; p. 10, Gate and token sampling
evidence.detail: A projected pooled stage vector is added to video tokens through alpha=0.2 sigmoid(beta). The gate is global, the vector sample-specific, and regularization constrains gate magnitude and relative residual scale.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Implementation Details; p. 10, Training details and Gate and token sampling
evidence.detail: The text specifies hardware, precision, AdamW settings, warmups, effective batches, gate settings and raw-frame target offsets. Stage I uses 1,000 updates; Stage II uses four epochs. Each runs once with seed 0 and uses its final checkpoint.

evidence.location: PDF p. 5, Closed-Loop Inference, Eqs. (15)–(16); p. 11, Closed-loop inference
evidence.detail: Deployment uses a causal 64-frame buffer with earliest-frame padding, followed by stage prediction, WAM prediction, action-chunk execution and renewed observation. Boundaries and target clips are training-only supervision.

Evaluation covers 50 tasks, two configurations and 100 episodes per task–configuration pair. Baseline numbers come from the Motus publication; the authors state a common closed-loop protocol for Motus and StageWAM.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Table 1, All tasks, Handover and Acquisition & lifting rows
evidence.detail: StageWAM/Motus success is 91.42/88.66 clean and 89.08/87.02 randomized overall. Handover is 96.50/82.00 and 93.50/68.00. Acquisition/lifting favors Motus in both settings. Categories use unweighted task means.

evidence.location: PDF p. 6, Table 2, Overall column and Ablation Study
evidence.detail: Overall success is 87.23 without JEPA, 89.89 with current-frame-only guidance, 89.98 without Stage-I training, 89.88 without gate regularizers and 90.25 for StageWAM. The prose defines each intervention.

The prose reports Motus-to-StageWAM mean lengths of 156.28 to 132.80 across all rollouts and 79.57 to 74.82 among successes, with reductions of 15.02% and 5.97%. Success terminates an episode; failures run to the horizon.

evidence.location: PDF p. 11, Table 5 and Stage-boundary and slice-overlap diagnostics
evidence.detail: Mean stage length is 44.74 frames and median length 34; 81.72% of intervals are shorter than 64 frames. Current–target slice overlap is 86.77% clean and 86.34% randomized. The authors characterize supervision as temporally contextual.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Table 3; p. 11, Real-world evaluation and Scoring
evidence.detail: LIFT2 evaluation covers cube grasping and bimanual power-strip operation, with 20 trials per task. Terminal-state progress scores range from zero to 100; specified safety failures receive zero.

evidence.location: PDF p. 10, Table 4; p. 11, Real-world evaluation—Results
evidence.detail: Separate task models use 50 cube and 116 power-strip trajectories. StageWAM scores 45.00 and 51.00, averaging 48.00; π0.5 scores 33.50 and 49.50, averaging 41.50. Only averages are reported.

evidence.location: PDF p. 13, Table 6, Average row and caption; p. 6, Table 1, All tasks row
evidence.detail: The two tables print different clean aggregate values for GO-1 and X-VLA, while Motus and StageWAM agree. Table 6 states that its final row preserves printed baseline aggregates from Motus.

evidence.location: PDF pp. 5–6, Main Results discussion; p. 7, Conclusion
evidence.detail: The authors associate gains with task-progress relations, identify contact geometry and timing as remaining challenges, and propose lower inference latency and representations combining task progress with fine-grained manipulation information.
